thread.title: Disability discrimination complaint preceded Chicago health commissioner's exit
thread.title_full: Disability discrimination complaint preceded Chicago health commissioner's exit

author: nbcchicago
title: Disability discrimination complaint preceded Chicago health commissioner's exit
text:
A month after Mayor Brandon Johnson asked Chicago’s public health commissioner to resign, new documents reveal what preceded her departure.
New documents tell the story of why Mayor Brandon Johnson asked the CDPH commissioner to resign, and NBC 5 Investigates’ Rose Schmidt has more details.
A month after Mayor Brandon Johnson asked Chicago's public health commissioner to resign, new documents reveal what preceded her departure. Less than three years after Johnson tapped Dr. Olusimbo"Simbo" Ige to lead the Department of Public Health, he asked for her letter of resignation. NBC 5 Investigates obtained documents showing an employee filed a complaint alleging disability discrimination. The documents reveal the city found Ige violated a city policy, and she was asked to resign a month later.
Heavily redacted city documents show Ige violated the Equal Employment Opportunity policy. It started with a complaint filed by a city employee who requested an accommodation due to their disability.
However, there was a delay in getting the accommodation, leading to"significant stress and anxiety" and a"financial burden.
" The investigation report noted because of the delays in the accommodation and the harm suffered by the employee, Ige's actions violated the EEO policy. Ige told NBC 5 the findings were never discussed with her. As for the allegations, she said asking questions about accommodations is allowed, and she disputes causing a delay.
"Accommodations are determined by the EEO office and I am notified for awareness. My sign off is to acknowledge receipt of the determination. I have signed all accommodation notices that have come to me," Ige told NBC 5 in an email. Separate from the HR investigation, there was a controversy over how Ige handled federal COVID-19 grants.
The Chicago Tribune reported she voluntarily sent $94 million back to the federal government, but she disputes that, telling NBC 5 the grants can only be reimbursed for expenses incurred. On Tuesday, Johnson touted a public health milestone in Chicago: Life expectancy in Chicago has reached an all-time high: 79.5 years. Ige said she helped reach the milestone, along with reducing mortality rates and opioid overdoses.
A medical doctor trained in Nigeria, Ige explained why she transitioned to public health in a YouTube video posted by the mayor's office last March.
"If I wanted to make the most impact, I needed to transition from just treating to preventing, and public health is where prevention happens," Ige said. Hannah Matzke, a former CDPH employee, said she was interviewed as a witness in the HR investigation.
"I had seen things that really disproportionately made it more difficult for people with disabilities to work there," Matzke said. Matzke told NBC 5's Mary Ann Ahern multiple employees asked for accommodations after the team moved to a different building.
"The office was often over 80 degrees on top of awful lighting, a lot of noise, echoes because you are within touching distance of the people you're on these Zoom calls with," Matzke explained. Ige believes the HR investigation was"part of a systematic effort to discredit" her and alleges it's part of a larger pattern of going after staff who don't agree with the mayor's administration.
When NBC 5 asked Johnson about that, he deflected, saying instead he’s focused on his public health agenda.
"I'm going to continue to lead with that tenacity, and there's still more work to be done until we close the gap effectively," Johnson said.
